title: King Pasenadi and the Mountains
hookLine: at funerals people say 'i can't believe it'; Atisha's first root says what everyone knows and nobody feels
carry: atisha's first root: death is certain, so live well
tomorrow: how fast is a life actually running out?

cards: At funerals, one sentence comes up again and again by the coffin: I can't believe it. Even when the person was old. Even when everyone knew.
So why do we act like we might escape? Buddhist teachers give a simple answer. We know death as a fact about everyone, and almost never as a fact about me.
The first root is about closing that gap.

teach.b: Tibetan Buddhism carries a teaching on death handed down from Atisha, an Indian teacher who went to Tibet. It has three roots: death is certain; when is uncertain; at death, only the practice helps. Today, the first.
Death is certain. No one escapes it. The suttas make the point with a picture.
King Pasenadi comes to the Buddha in the middle of the day, busy with royal business.

teach.h: MOUNTAINS ROLLING IN, ALL FOUR SIDES.
teach.b: The Buddha asks him: suppose trusted men came from the east, the west, the north and the south, each saying a mountain as high as the sky is rolling this way, crushing every living thing. What would you do?
And the king says: what else could I do, but live by the teaching and do good? Then the Buddha tells him: aging and death are rolling in on you like that.
The king admits his elephants, chariots, soldiers and treasure can't fight it.
The Dhammapada says it another way: not in the sky, not in the sea, not in a mountain cave is there a place where death can't reach. The root isn't meant to frighten.
It moves the fact from everyone to me, and then, gently, to everyone I love.
And at a funeral it gives something solid: no one failed by dying. It came to the king. It comes to all.
What's left is the king's answer: live well, do good.

how: In Tibetan Buddhism the three roots of death reflection are taught near the start of the lamrim, the graded path; at many Buddhist funerals, monks or lay leaders chant verses on impermanence while family and friends listen.

o: a belief that death is fixed on a set date
the first root: no one escapes dying
a vow to face death without any fear at all

games.q: the first root — tap the pairs.
p: rolling in from all four sides
live by the teaching, do good

s: if someone was old, their death should hurt less
people say 'i can't believe it' even then. the root is certain for everyone; grief still comes.
in the sutta, King Pasenadi says his army and treasure can't fight aging and death
elephants, chariots, soldiers and wealth: none of it holds back the mountain.
Atisha's first root is meant to make people afraid
it moves the fact from everyone to me, and leaves the king's answer: live well, do good.

games.q: at a funeral, a cousin keeps asking what the family should have done differently. the doctors did everything. which answer does the first root give?
o: nobody failed by dying; it came to the king, it comes to all.
someone always could have done more; that's why it hurts.
it's better not to talk about death at a funeral at all.
games.why: death is certain. the root takes away the blame, and leaves the living with the king's answer: live well, do good.

practice: Write one line by hand: death is certain. Under it, write your own name, and then one name you love. Rest your eyes on the page while the bell runs, and if it gets heavy, add one more line underneath: and today is still here.

wordCard.voice: Death is certain: Atisha's first root. No one escapes it, not the king with his elephants, not anyone you know.

orig.note: Pali: death; the Dhammapada's word for death, sometimes pictured as a king or a hunter.

carryVoice: The line for today: Atisha's first root. Death is certain, so live well and do good, as the king answered. Four of thirty, done gently.

sources.ref: Samyutta Nikaya 3.25 (Pabbatopama Sutta: the simile of the mountains rolling in from the four quarters)
Dhammapada 128 (no place in sky, sea or mountain cleft where death cannot overcome)
Atisha's three roots of death contemplation, as taught in the Tibetan lamrim (e.g. Tsongkhapa's Great Treatise on the Stages of the Path; Gampopa's Jewel Ornament of Liberation)
